newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Asia-Pacific seen more dependent on Mideast oil.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Pacific seen more dependent on Mideast oil.

text.p: The Asia-Pacific region will become increasingly dependent on the Middle East for petroleum supplies and should develop stronger links with the region, Malaysia's acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Monday.
The growing role of gas in the global energy equation underscores the importance of the Middle East as a long-term energy supplier, Anwar told the Asia Oil and Gas Conference.
"Some have even said that growing dependence on the Middle East is inescapable. Without a doubt, West Asia is poised to have a bigger impact on the booming Asia Pacific," he said.

Considering the Middle East's importance "it is surprising that the ties between our two regions have not been stronger", Anwar said. "We should be removing the barriers that have impeded progress in our relationship."
"Perhaps the time has come to set up a forum for the two regions to address issues of mutual interest, starting with oil and gas," Anwar said.

Anwar said the national oil companies of the Middle East should break out of their traditional roles and markets, and join with national oil companies in the Asia-Pacific region to compete with the global giants.
"The major players are rationalising themselves through mergers to increase their global strength and competitiveness.
"But there is a new breed of national oil companies emerging from the Asia Pacific as significant players. Perhaps the Middle East Oil companies would do well to consider them as potential partners."
The basis for such a partnership should be in downstream activities, Anwar said.
"Interdependence between the Middle East and the Asia Pacific will become a fact of life, if it is not already," he said.
"In fact, many Middle Eastern national oil companies have broken new ground in the Asia Pacific. And the prospect of growing links presents exciting possibilities."
Asian oil markets will become increasingly dependent on Middle East petroleum because at current rates of production, Asia's reserves are expected to be depleted within 15 years.

Under this scenario, natural gas will play a more prominent role, Anwar said. Its share of global primary energy consumption has already increased over the past two decades to 23 percent from 17 percent.
The Middle East and countries from the former Soviet Union account for 70 percent of global production but only 33 percent of consumption.
By contrast, the major industrialised nations hold only 11 percent of proven reserves but account for 51 percent of consumption, Anwar said.
"Supplies appear to be situated further and further away from the leading consumers," he said.
